segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way, wives, submit to your own husbands, so that even if some of them disobey the word, they may be won over without a word by the conduct of their wives,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: when they observe your pure and reverent conduct.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let your adornment not be the outward kind—braiding hair, putting on gold jewelry, or wearing clothes—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the hidden person of the heart, with the imperishable quality of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great value in God’s sight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is how the holy women of the past who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, submitting to their own husbands,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You have become her children if you do good and do not fear anything that terrifies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Husbands, in the same way, live with your wives with understanding, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, and as fellow heirs also of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finally, all of you, be of one mind, sympathetic, loving toward your brothers and sisters, tenderhearted, and humble,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not repaying evil with evil or insult with insult, but on the contrary blessing, because you were called to this, so that you might inherit a blessing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Whoever wants to love life and see good days must keep the tongue from evil and the lips from speaking deceit,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: must turn away from evil and do good, must seek peace and pursue it.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their plea, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And who is going to harm you if you become zealous for what is good?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But even if you should suffer because of righteousness, you are blessed. Have no fear of them, and do not be troubled,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always ready to make a defense to anyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but with gentleness and reverence, keeping a good conscience, so that those who disparage your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame in the very matter in which you are slandered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God’s will, than for doing evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring you to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in which he also went and made proclamation to the spirits in prison,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who had once disobeyed, when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah while an ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight people—were saved through water.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you as well—not the removal of dirt from the flesh but the pledge of a good conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who is at God’s right hand, having gone into heaven, with angels and authorities and powers made subject to him.

notes.note: “Meek” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone who is gentle and not self-assertive, and “gentle” or “humble” is the mainstream modern rendering. The related noun is rendered “gentleness” in verse 16.

notes.traditional: as long as ye do well
notes.note: The Greek has two participles (“doing good and not fearing”) whose relation to “you have become her children” is left open. They may state a condition, as here and in most translations, or describe how the readers show themselves her children (“by doing good”). Sarah calls Abraham “lord” in Genesis 18:12, and the closing words echo Proverbs 3:25.

“Vessel” was a familiar image for a human being as a created, fragile thing, or for the body. The comparative “weaker” implies that the husband is a vessel too. The weakness is usually understood as physical strength or social vulnerability rather than moral or intellectual inferiority, and the verse goes on to call wives “fellow heirs.” Some translations paraphrase as “the weaker partner.”

Verses 10–12 quote Psalm 34:12–16 (33:13–17 in the Septuagint numbering) with small adaptations and without an introductory formula. The opening “For” is the letter’s own link to the preceding instruction.

notes.traditional: be not afraid of their terror
notes.note: Literally “do not fear their fear.” The words come from Isaiah 8:12, where the sense is “do not fear what this people fears,” and some translations keep that sense here. In this context of hostility most interpreters take it as “do not be afraid of them” or “of their threats.” Isaiah continues “the Lord himself you shall regard as holy,” which the next verse applies to Christ.

notes.phrase: honor Christ the Lord as holy
notes.traditional: sanctify the Lord God; sanctify Christ as Lord
notes.note: The traditional “sanctify” hides the link with “holy,” and Christ cannot be made holy; the sense, as the standard lexicons give it, is to acknowledge and treat as holy. The Greek can also be construed “honor Christ as Lord,” as several translations have it. The wording adapts Isaiah 8:13, where “the Lord” is Israel’s God.

Later manuscripts read “the Lord God” instead of “the Lord Christ,” and that reading lies behind the King James Version. The earliest witnesses have “Christ,” and modern critical editions follow them.

Many manuscripts, including early ones, read “died” in place of “suffered,” and the manuscripts are also divided between “bring you to God” and “bring us to God.” The edition translated here reads “suffered” and “you.” “Suffered” fits the letter’s usual vocabulary and the argument of verse 17, and the verse in any case goes on to speak of Christ being put to death.

The Greek sets “flesh” and “spirit” in exact parallel, with no preposition. The phrase may mean that Christ was made alive in the realm of the spirit, that is, in his risen mode of existence, or that he was made alive by God’s Spirit (“by the Spirit”). The parallel with “in the flesh” favors the first. Many recent interpreters take “made alive” to refer to the resurrection.

notes.traditional: preached unto the spirits in prison
notes.note: This is one of the most disputed verses in the New Testament. The most widely held scholarly view today is that the “spirits” are the rebellious angelic beings of Genesis 6:1–4, whose imprisonment is described in Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch, and that the risen Christ announced his victory to them. Others take them to be the human dead of Noah’s generation, or hold that Christ preached through Noah to people now in prison. The verb means “proclaim” and does not say what was announced; “in which” could also be read “at which time.”

The Greek word often rendered “soul” is used here, as frequently in the Septuagint, simply to count individuals. “Souls” could suggest to a modern reader that only an immaterial part of them was rescued. Most modern translations have “persons” or “people.”

notes.phrase: the pledge of a good conscience toward God
notes.traditional: the answer of a good conscience toward God; an appeal to God for a good conscience
notes.note: The noun occurs only here in the New Testament and its meaning is disputed. It is related to a verb meaning “ask,” which supports “appeal” or “request”: baptism as an appeal to God for a good conscience. In papyri, mostly somewhat later, the word-group is used of the formal question and answer that sealed a contract, which supports “pledge”: a commitment made to God from, or to keep, a good conscience. Both renderings have strong scholarly support, and the choice here is not certain.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the household codes, Romans 13 and Christological texts, and translators vary between “submit,” “be subject,” “be subordinate” and “accept the authority of,” with real differences in tone.
A key word in 1–2 Peter and elsewhere that the KJV rendered “conversation” and modern versions split among “conduct,” “behavior” and “way of life.”
Translators divide between “disobey” and “refuse to believe” across John, Acts, Romans, Hebrews and 1 Peter, and the choice affects how unbelief is portrayed.
Its range (body, mortal human existence, sinful nature) is rendered very differently across versions, especially in Paul, and readers are misled when the English shifts without notice.
“Preach” versus “proclaim” needs a single policy, since “preach” now suggests a sermon in church rather than a herald’s public announcement.
